\chapter{Farewells}
\label{ch:farewells}
\hlchaptermodality{4}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can end a French conversation politely and choose a farewell that fits the situation.}

You can open a French conversation; now close it. French has one plain goodbye and a small family of soft ones, all built the same way — the preposition à (“to”) followed by a time word — and this chapter also teaches the accents, the cedilla and the trema you have been reading all along.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[au revoir]{au revoir — \textquotedblleft{}goodbye,\textquotedblright{} i.e. \textquotedblleft{}until we see each other again\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:FR-C04-au-revoir}



\begin{quote}
You can open a French conversation; now close it. The standard goodbye is \textbf{au revoir} — and where Spanish \emph{adiós} commends you \emph{to God}, French makes a promise to \textbf{see you again}.
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \texttt{r-uvular} — two guttural French \emph{r}'s: \emph{oh ruh-VWAHR}.
  \item \texttt{vowel-oi} — \textbf{-voir} = \emph{vwahr} (the \emph{oi} = \emph{wa}, as in \emph{soir} from Chapter 1).
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{au revoir} is \textbf{au} + \textbf{revoir} = \textquotedblleft{}at the \textbf{re-seeing}\textquotedblright{}:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{au} = \textquotedblleft{}at/to the\textquotedblright{} (a fusion of \emph{à} + \emph{le}).
  \item \textbf{revoir} = \textquotedblleft{}to see again\textquotedblright{} = \textbf{re-} (\textquotedblleft{}again\textquotedblright{}) + \textbf{voir} (\textquotedblleft{}to see\textquotedblright{}).
\end{itemize}

So \emph{au revoir} literally means \textbf{\textquotedblleft{}until the seeing-again\textquotedblright{}} — a small promise that this isn't the end. It's built on \textbf{voir}, from Latin \textbf{vidēre}, \textquotedblleft{}to see\textquotedblright{} — one of the richest roots in English:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{vis}ion, \textbf{vis}ible, \textbf{vis}it, \textbf{vis}a, \textbf{view}, \textbf{video} (\textquotedblleft{}I see\textquotedblright{}).
  \item \textbf{re-vise} (\textquotedblleft{}look again\textquotedblright{}), \textbf{e-vid}ent (\textquotedblleft{}seen out\textquotedblright{}), \textbf{pro-vide}, \textbf{super-vise}, \textbf{sur-vey}.
\end{itemize}
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{culture}
Here's a satisfying cross-language pair: \textbf{German says the exact same thing.} \emph{Auf Wiedersehen} = \emph{auf} (\textquotedblleft{}on\textquotedblright{}) + \emph{wieder} (\textquotedblleft{}again\textquotedblright{}) + \emph{sehen} (\textquotedblleft{}to see\textquotedblright{}) = \textquotedblleft{}on the seeing-again.\textquotedblright{} French and German, side by side, both promise a \textbf{re-seeing}; Spanish \emph{adiós} instead commends you \emph{to God}. Same moment, two different pictures.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}au revoir\textquotedblright{} — \emph{oh ruh-VWAHR}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}au revoir\textquotedblright{} then English \textquotedblleft{}vision, revise, video\textquotedblright{} — the \emph{vidēre} family
  \item French \emph{au revoir} and German \emph{auf Wiedersehen} — both \textquotedblleft{}see you again\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \emph{au revoir} literally mean? (\textquotedblleft{}Until the seeing-again.\textquotedblright{}) What Latin verb is \emph{voir} from, and two English cousins? (\emph{vidēre} — vision, video, revise.) Which other language builds its goodbye the same \textquotedblleft{}see again\textquotedblright{} way? (German \emph{auf Wiedersehen}.) Next: \textbf{à plus tard}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[à plus tard]{à plus tard — the casual \textquotedblleft{}see you later\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:FR-C04-a-plus-tard}



\begin{quote}
The everyday, friendly \textquotedblleft{}see you later\textquotedblright{} is \textbf{à plus tard} — and among friends it shrinks to just \textbf{à plus} (\emph{ah PLUSS}, and here you \emph{do} sound the final \emph{s}). It's the French twin of Spanish \emph{hasta luego}.
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \texttt{silent-final} — in the full phrase, \emph{plus} is \emph{ploo} (silent \emph{s}): \emph{ah ploo TAR}. But in the clipped \textbf{à plus}, the \emph{s} is pronounced: \emph{ah PLUSS}.
  \item \textbf{tard} = \emph{tar} (silent \emph{d}).
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{à plus tard} = literally \textquotedblleft{}to more late\textquotedblright{} $\to$ \textquotedblleft{}see you later.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{à} = \textquotedblleft{}to / at\textquotedblright{} (Latin \emph{ad}) — French's all-purpose farewell preposition, the way Spanish leans on \emph{hasta}: \emph{à} + a time = a soft goodbye.
  \item \textbf{plus} = \textquotedblleft{}more,\textquotedblright{} from Latin \textbf{plūs} — the \emph{plus} you already write in English (and the \emph{plu}- of \emph{plural}, \emph{surplus}).
  \item \textbf{tard} = \textquotedblleft{}late,\textquotedblright{} from Latin \textbf{tarde}, \textquotedblleft{}slowly, late.\textquotedblright{} English keeps it in \textbf{tardy} and \textbf{retard} (\textquotedblleft{}hold back, make late\textquotedblright{}).
\end{itemize}

So \emph{à plus tard} is \textquotedblleft{}until more-late\textquotedblright{} — see you at some later point.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{culture}
Spanish inherited that identical Latin \emph{tarde} — the word you met in Chapter 2 — but the two languages grew it in different directions. French kept it meaning \textbf{late} (\emph{tard}); Spanish grew it into \textbf{afternoon} (\emph{tarde}). One Latin word, two everyday meanings. And where French leans on \textbf{à} for its soft goodbyes, Spanish leans on \textbf{hasta} (\textquotedblleft{}until\textquotedblright{}): \emph{hasta luego} is the twin of \emph{à plus tard}.
\end{culture}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the \textquotedblleft{}à …\textquotedblright{} farewells}]
French's soft goodbyes are all \textbf{à} + a time word — mirror this against Spanish \emph{hasta}:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{French} & \textbf{Spanish} & \textbf{\textquotedblleft{}until / to …\textquotedblright{}} \\
\midrule
\textbf{à plus tard} / à plus & hasta luego & later \\
\textbf{à bientôt} & hasta pronto & soon \\
\textbf{à demain} & hasta mañana & tomorrow \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}à plus tard\textquotedblright{} (\emph{ah ploo TAR}), then clipped \textquotedblleft{}à plus\textquotedblright{} (\emph{ah PLUSS})
  \item \textquotedblleft{}tard\textquotedblright{} then Spanish \textquotedblleft{}tarde\textquotedblright{} — the same Latin \emph{tarde}, \textquotedblleft{}late\textquotedblright{}
  \item English \textquotedblleft{}tardy, retard\textquotedblright{} — held back, late
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \emph{à plus tard} literally mean? (\textquotedblleft{}To more late.\textquotedblright{}) What Spanish word is \emph{tard} identical to at the root, and what does each mean now? (\emph{tarde} — French \textquotedblleft{}late\textquotedblright{}, Spanish \textquotedblleft{}afternoon\textquotedblright{}.) What preposition carries French's soft goodbyes, like Spanish \emph{hasta}? (\emph{à}.) Next: \textbf{à bientôt}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[à bientôt]{à bientôt — \textquotedblleft{}see you soon\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:FR-C04-a-bientot}



\begin{quote}
For when you'll genuinely meet again shortly: \textbf{à bientôt}, \textquotedblleft{}see you soon\textquotedblright{} — the French twin of Spanish \emph{hasta pronto}. It hides a word you already know from Chapter 1: \textbf{bien}.
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \texttt{nasal-in} — \textbf{bien} = \emph{byan}, nasal (your Chapter 1 sound).
  \item \textbf{bientôt} = \emph{byan-TOH}; the circumflex on \emph{ô} just marks a long \emph{o}, and the final \emph{t} is silent. Whole phrase: \emph{ah byan-TOH}.
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{à bientôt} = \textquotedblleft{}to soon\textquotedblright{} $\to$ \textquotedblleft{}see you soon.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{à} = \textquotedblleft{}to\textquotedblright{} (the farewell preposition again).
  \item \textbf{bientôt} = \textquotedblleft{}soon,\textquotedblright{} and it's a compound you can pull apart: - \textbf{bien} = \textquotedblleft{}well\textquotedblright{} (Chapter 1 — from Latin \emph{bene}, the \emph{bene} of \emph{benefit}). - \textbf{tôt} = \textquotedblleft{}early / soon.\textquotedblright{} - Together, \emph{bien + tôt} = \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{well-soon}\textquotedblright{} $\to$ \emph{quite soon}. (French loves gluing \emph{bien} onto words for emphasis — \emph{bientôt} \textquotedblleft{}soon\textquotedblright{}, \emph{bienvenue} \textquotedblleft{}welcome\textquotedblright{} = \textquotedblleft{}well-come\textquotedblright{}.)
\end{itemize}

The circumflex \textbf{ô} is itself a little history lesson: a circumflex usually marks an \textbf{s that dropped out} (\emph{hôtel} was \emph{hostel}, \emph{forêt} was \emph{forest}). \emph{tôt} came from an older \emph{tost} — so the hat on \emph{ô} is the ghost of a lost \emph{s}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: bien, the intensifier}]
You met \emph{bien} as \textquotedblleft{}well\textquotedblright{} (an answer to \emph{ça va?}). Here it's doing a second job: \textbf{gluing onto another word to strengthen it} — \emph{bien + tôt} = \textquotedblleft{}soon indeed.\textquotedblright{} Same word, new trick.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}à bientôt\textquotedblright{} — \emph{ah byan-TOH}
  \item pull it apart — \textquotedblleft{}bien\textquotedblright{} (well) + \textquotedblleft{}tôt\textquotedblright{} (early) = bientôt (soon)
  \item \textquotedblleft{}à bientôt\textquotedblright{} = Spanish \textquotedblleft{}hasta pronto\textquotedblright{} — see you soon
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What two words hide inside \emph{bientôt}? (\emph{bien} \textquotedblleft{}well\textquotedblright{} + \emph{tôt} \textquotedblleft{}early\textquotedblright{} $\to$ soon.) What does the circumflex on \emph{ô} usually mark? (A dropped \emph{s} — \emph{tost} $\to$ \emph{tôt}.) What's the Spanish equivalent of \emph{à bientôt}? (\emph{hasta pronto}.) Next: \textbf{à demain}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[à demain]{à demain — \textquotedblleft{}see you tomorrow\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:FR-C04-a-demain}



\begin{quote}
Parting for the day: \textbf{à demain}, \textquotedblleft{}until tomorrow\textquotedblright{} — the twin of Spanish \emph{hasta mañana}. And \emph{demain} shares a hidden root with \emph{mañana} that's worth seeing.
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \texttt{nasal-in} — \textbf{demain} = \emph{duh-MAN}: the \emph{-ain} is a nasal (like \emph{pain}, \emph{main}); the final consonant is silent. \emph{ah duh-MAN}.
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{à demain} = \textquotedblleft{}to tomorrow\textquotedblright{} $\to$ \textquotedblleft{}see you tomorrow.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{à} = \textquotedblleft{}to\textquotedblright{} (the farewell preposition, one last time).
  \item \textbf{demain} = \textquotedblleft{}tomorrow,\textquotedblright{} from Latin \textbf{dē māne}, \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{from the morning}\textquotedblright{}: - \textbf{dē} = \textquotedblleft{}from\textquotedblright{} · \textbf{māne} = \textquotedblleft{}in the morning.\textquotedblright{} - The next \textquotedblleft{}morning\textquotedblright{} is \emph{tomorrow} $\to$ \emph{de mane} fused into \textbf{demain}.
\end{itemize}

English keeps \emph{māne} too, in the poetic \textbf{matins} (morning prayers) and \textbf{matinée} (a \emph{morning}/daytime show).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{culture}
Spanish \emph{mañana} (\textquotedblleft{}tomorrow / morning\textquotedblright{}) comes from Latin \emph{(hōra) maneana} — built on the \textbf{same} \emph{māne}, \textquotedblleft{}morning.\textquotedblright{} So French \textbf{demain} and Spanish \textbf{mañana} are cousins through one Latin word: both turn \textquotedblleft{}morning\textquotedblright{} into \textquotedblleft{}tomorrow,\textquotedblright{} just assembled differently — French says \emph{from-morning}, Spanish says \emph{morning-ish hour}.
\end{culture}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the \textquotedblleft{}à …\textquotedblright{} farewells, complete}]
Your French soft-goodbye set, mapped to Spanish:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{French} & \textbf{Spanish} & \textbf{when} \\
\midrule
\textbf{à plus tard} / à plus & hasta luego & later (default) \\
\textbf{à bientôt} & hasta pronto & soon \\
\textbf{à demain} & hasta mañana & tomorrow \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

…and \textbf{au revoir} for the plain goodbye.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}à demain\textquotedblright{} — \emph{ah duh-MAN}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}demain\textquotedblright{} $\leftarrow$ \emph{de mane} \textquotedblleft{}from morning\textquotedblright{}; Spanish \textquotedblleft{}mañana\textquotedblright{} $\leftarrow$ \emph{maneana} — same \emph{māne}
  \item the three \textquotedblleft{}à …\textquotedblright{} goodbyes — à plus tard / à bientôt / à demain
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \emph{demain} literally come from? (\emph{dē māne} — \textquotedblleft{}from the morning.\textquotedblright{}) What Spanish word shares that \emph{māne} root? (\emph{mañana}.) Which French goodbye for parting until tomorrow? (\emph{à demain}.) Next: put the farewells together.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{Practice — saying goodbye in French}

\label{lesson:FR-C04-practice}



\begin{quote}
No new words. The farewells — \emph{au revoir} and the three \emph{à …} goodbyes — now close a real conversation and fold back into everything since \emph{salut}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn: choosing the right goodbye}
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{you're…} & \textbf{say} \\
\midrule
parting plainly / politely & \textbf{au revoir} \\
expecting to meet again shortly & \textbf{à bientôt} \\
casual \textquotedblleft{}see you\textquotedblright{} & \textbf{à plus (tard)} \\
leaving for the day & \textbf{à demain} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\subsection*{The exchange, start to finish}
Everything from the French Chapters 1–4:

\begin{quote}
— Salut ! Je m'appelle Chloé. Comment tu t'appelles ? — Je m'appelle Marc. Enchanté. — Ça va ? — Ça va bien, merci, et toi ? — Très bien. Bon… \textbf{à demain}, Marc. — Oui, \textbf{à demain}, Chloé. \textbf{Au revoir !}
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built this chapter}]
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{au revoir} — the plain goodbye (\textquotedblleft{}until the seeing-again\textquotedblright{}; the \emph{voir} / \emph{vidēre} family; twin of German \emph{auf Wiedersehen}).
  \item \textbf{à plus tard / à bientôt / à demain} — later / soon / tomorrow, all \textbf{à} + a time, mirroring Spanish's \textbf{hasta}.
\end{itemize}
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the full conversation, both voices — \emph{salut} to \emph{au revoir}
  \item pick the goodbye — a friend you'll see tomorrow? (à demain); a polite plain goodbye? (au revoir)
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} Run the exchange, greeting to goodbye, without stopping.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \emph{au revoir} literally promise? (A \emph{re-seeing} — \textquotedblleft{}until we see again.\textquotedblright{}) Which preposition carries French's soft goodbyes? (\emph{à} — like Spanish \emph{hasta}.) You can now hold a whole short French exchange, hello to goodbye. Next chapter: numbers, or everyday courtesies (\emph{s'il vous plaît}).
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[é è ê]{é è ê — the three hats on \emph{e}, and the one that hides an \emph{s}}

\label{lesson:FR-W01-accents}



\begin{quote}
French sprinkles little marks over its vowels, and they are \textbf{not} decoration — each does a specific job. You've read them since \emph{enchanté} and \emph{très}. Three of them ride on \emph{e}, and one of the three hides a word you already know in English.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: the three accents, and what they do}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{é} — \emph{accent aigu} (rising stroke, like Spanish's). It fixes the sound: \textbf{é = a crisp \textquotedblleft{}ay\textquotedblright{}} (no glide). \emph{café}, \emph{enchanté}, \emph{été} (\textquotedblleft{}summer\textquotedblright{}).
  \item \textbf{è} — \emph{accent grave} (falling stroke). \textbf{è = an open \textquotedblleft{}eh\textquotedblright{}} as in \emph{bed}. \emph{très} (\textquotedblleft{}very\textquotedblright{}), \emph{mère} (\textquotedblleft{}mother\textquotedblright{}), \emph{père}. The grave also just \textbf{separates look-alikes}: \emph{a} (\textquotedblleft{}has\textquotedblright{}) vs \textbf{à} (\textquotedblleft{}to\textquotedblright{}); \emph{ou} (\textquotedblleft{}or\textquotedblright{}) vs \textbf{où} (\textquotedblleft{}where\textquotedblright{}) — same job as Spanish \emph{tu/tú}.
  \item \textbf{ê} — \emph{accent circonflexe} (a little hat). This one is a \textbf{fossil}.
\end{itemize}

\begin{culture}
Centuries ago French dropped an \emph{s} before certain consonants, and left a \textbf{hat} where it used to stand. English, having borrowed the older form, usually \textbf{still has that s} — so the circumflex is a decoder ring between the two languages:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{French (hat)} & \textbf{the lost \emph{s}} & \textbf{English kept it} \\
\midrule
\textbf{forêt} & forest & \textbf{forest} \\
\textbf{hôpital} & hospital & \textbf{hospital} \\
\textbf{île} & isle & \textbf{isle / island} \\
\textbf{bête} & beste & \textbf{beast} \\
\textbf{fête} & feste & \textbf{feast} \\
\textbf{pâte} & paste & \textbf{paste / pasta} \\
\textbf{goût} & gust & (Latin \emph{gustus}, cf. \emph{gusto}) \\
\textbf{être} & estre & (Latin \emph{stāre}, cf. \emph{stare/estar}) \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

So when you meet a circumflex, \textbf{mentally slot an \emph{s} back in} and an English cousin often appears. \emph{Hôpital $\to$ hospital.} It's the single most useful reading trick in French spelling.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Writing: the three accents}
All three are small strokes \textbf{above} the vowel: \textbf{é} leans right (up-stroke), \textbf{è} leans left (down-stroke), \textbf{ê} is a little peak (\textasciicircum{}). Get the \emph{lean} right — \emph{é} and \emph{è} are different sounds, so the direction matters.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}é\textquotedblright{} = \emph{ay} (\emph{café}), \textquotedblleft{}è\textquotedblright{} = \emph{eh} (\emph{très}) — hear the two sounds
  \item forêt $\to$ forest, hôpital $\to$ hospital, île $\to$ isle — put the \emph{s} back
  \item \textquotedblleft{}à\textquotedblright{} vs \textquotedblleft{}a\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}où\textquotedblright{} vs \textquotedblleft{}ou\textquotedblright{} — the grave that only separates
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which accent makes \emph{e} say \textquotedblleft{}ay,\textquotedblright{} and which \textquotedblleft{}eh\textquotedblright{}? (\emph{é} aigu = ay; \emph{è} grave = eh.) What does the circumflex \textbf{ê} usually mark, and how do you use it? (A lost \emph{s} — slot it back to find the English cousin: \emph{forêt} $\to$ forest.) Next writing lesson: the little hook under \emph{c} — the \textbf{cédille}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ç]{ç — the little tail that softens \emph{c}}

\label{lesson:FR-W02-cedille}



\begin{quote}
You've seen it in \textbf{français} and \textbf{garçon}. The \textbf{cédille} is the tiny hook under a \emph{c} — \textbf{ç} — and it exists to solve one specific spelling problem.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: the problem the cedilla solves}
In French (as in Latin, Italian, Spanish), \textbf{c is soft (an \emph{s} sound) before \emph{e} and \emph{i}}, but \textbf{hard (a \emph{k}) before \emph{a}, \emph{o}, \emph{u}}:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{ce}, \emph{ci} $\to$ soft: \emph{ceci} = \emph{suh-SEE}.
  \item \emph{ca}, \emph{co}, \emph{cu} $\to$ hard: \emph{car}, \emph{comme}, \emph{cure} = \emph{k}.
\end{itemize}

So \textquotedblleft{}franc-ais\textquotedblright{} would read \emph{frank-ay} — wrong. To force the \textbf{soft} \emph{s} before \emph{a/o/u}, French adds the hook: \textbf{ç}.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{français} = \emph{frahn-\textbf{SEH}} (not "frank-").
  \item \textbf{garçon} = \emph{gar-\textbf{SOHN}} (\textquotedblleft{}boy\textquotedblright{}).
  \item \textbf{ça} = \emph{sa} (\textquotedblleft{}that\textquotedblright{} — the \emph{ça} of \emph{ça va?}).
  \item \textbf{reçu} = \emph{ruh-\textbf{SU}} (\textquotedblleft{}received\textquotedblright{}).
\end{itemize}

The rule is tidy: \textbf{ç only ever appears before a, o, u} — never before \emph{e/i}, where \emph{c} is already soft and the hook would be pointless.

\begin{cousinweb}
The \emph{cédille} is literally \textbf{\textquotedblleft{}a little \emph{z}.\textquotedblright{}} Its name is Spanish \textbf{zedilla} (\textquotedblleft{}little zeta\textquotedblright{}) — medieval scribes wrote a small subscript \textbf{z} under the \emph{c} to say \textquotedblleft{}pronounce this like \emph{z/s}, not \emph{k}.\textquotedblright{} Over time the little \emph{z} shrank into the hook you write today. So \textbf{ç = c + a ghost z.} (Spanish later dropped it; French and Portuguese kept it — \emph{ç} is alive in \emph{português} itself.)
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Writing: the cedilla}
Write a normal \textbf{c}, then add a small \textbf{hook curling left off the bottom}, like a tiny \emph{5}'s tail. Only ever under \emph{c}, only before \emph{a/o/u}.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}français\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}garçon\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}ça\textquotedblright{} — the ç forcing a soft \emph{s}
  \item imagine no cédille — \textquotedblleft{}franc-ais\textquotedblright{} as \emph{frank-ay} — that's what it prevents
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does the cédille do, and before which letters does it appear? (Keeps \emph{c} soft (\emph{s}) — only before \emph{a, o, u}.) What is the hook, historically? (A shrunken subscript \emph{z} — Spanish \emph{zedilla}, \textquotedblleft{}little z\textquotedblright{}.) Next writing lesson: the two dots — the \textbf{tréma}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ï ë ü]{ï ë ü — the two dots that say \textquotedblleft{}say me on my own\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:FR-W03-trema}



\begin{quote}
The last French mark: two little dots over a vowel — the \textbf{tréma} (English calls it a \emph{diaeresis}). It answers one question the reader would otherwise get wrong: \textbf{do these two vowels blend, or not?}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: the problem the trema solves}
French loves to fuse vowel pairs into one sound: \emph{ai} = \emph{eh}, \emph{au} = \emph{oh}, \emph{ou} = \emph{oo}, \emph{oi} = \emph{wa}. Usually that's what you want. But sometimes two vowels really should be sounded \textbf{separately} — and the tréma is how the spelling says so: \textbf{\textquotedblleft{}break these apart; pronounce the marked vowel on its own.\textquotedblright{}}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{naïve} = \emph{na-\textbf{EEV}} (na-i, two syllables) — not \textquotedblleft{}nave.\textquotedblright{} (English kept the dots: \emph{naïve}.)
  \item \textbf{Noël} = \emph{no-\textbf{EL}} (\textquotedblleft{}Christmas\textquotedblright{}) — \emph{o} and \emph{e} separately, not \textquotedblleft{}nurl.\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textbf{maïs} = \emph{ma-\textbf{EES}} (\textquotedblleft{}corn\textquotedblright{}) — vs \textbf{mais} (\emph{meh}, \textquotedblleft{}but\textquotedblright{}). The two dots are the \emph{only} difference, and they flip the meaning.
  \item \textbf{Citroën}, \textbf{Israël}, \textbf{égoïste} — same rule: split the vowels.
\end{itemize}

So the tréma is the \textbf{opposite} of a blend instruction: where \emph{ai} says \textquotedblleft{}merge,\textquotedblright{} \emph{aï} says \textquotedblleft{}don't.\textquotedblright{}

\subsection*{Writing: the trema}
Two dots, side by side, \textbf{above} the vowel that starts its \textbf{own} sound — the \emph{second} vowel of the pair (na-\textbf{ï}-ve). (It looks like a German umlaut, but the job is different: German ä/ö/ü \emph{change} the vowel; the French tréma \emph{separates} it. Same two dots, opposite purpose — that's the next lesson.)

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}naïve\textquotedblright{} = na-EEV, \textquotedblleft{}Noël\textquotedblright{} = no-EL — two syllables each
  \item \textquotedblleft{}maïs\textquotedblright{} (ma-EES, corn) vs \textquotedblleft{}mais\textquotedblright{} (meh, but) — the dots flip it
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does the tréma tell you to do? (Pronounce the two vowels \textbf{separately}, not blended.) How is it different from a German umlaut? (Tréma \emph{separates} vowels; umlaut \emph{changes} a vowel's sound.) That's the French writing kit: \textbf{é è ê}, \textbf{ç}, and \textbf{ï ë}.
\end{tcolorbox}
